catalog_quote: Stress in Guna is very straightforward process. In roots, the stress always falls on the penultimate (second to last) syllable. (44) a. má.du ‘bread’ b. sá.pi ‘tree’ c. bá.ne ‘tomorrow’ d. dú.le ‘person’ e. bu.nó.lo ‘girl’ f. na.má.ke ‘to sing’ g. ar.bá.e ‘to work’ When a morpheme is added, the stress can shift if needed, either due to the addition of a morpheme that creates a three syllable word (41a), or due to elision (41c), which results in a two syllable word. sweep_summary: San Blas Kuna (sanb1242) is not in the catalog (audit422 full sweep already recorded S2-SCOPE-EXIT on Smith 2014 + Holmer 1947). The sweep's only title hit, Waller 2007 'Dolphin Signature Rhythms...' (Cognitive Semiotics), is an animal-cognition paper mis-tagged to Kuna: not relevant, priority none. The best first-hand stress statement remains Smith 2014 sec. 2.5 p. 48 (on file, read): root-penultimate main stress, suffixes can shift it, enclitics never carry it, secondary stress on the penult of long words; Holmer 1947:23 (on file, read) gives a weight-based account (accent on every heavy syllable), and Prince 1913:482 calls stress irregular. 34-48 of Giannelli, Marotta & Pacini 2002 Fonologia della lingua Cuna (Lincom LSNAL 42) -- print-only, priority high as the one dedicated metrical treatment; Holmer 1946 IJAL (DOI 10.1086/463913) paywalled, low priority; Sherzer 1975 not found. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Google Books and HathiTrust were all rate-limited/blocked (receipts saved). All fetches and receipts are under with updated.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root/stem (root + suffixes); suffixation and final-vowel elision re-place it on the new penult of the stem; clitics are outside the stress domain and never take main stress, so cliticised words can surface with antepenultimate or earlier main stress (ób-de=mar, án=mar=ga).
new_statements.secondary_stress: In words longer than four syllables a secondary stress is assigned on the penultimate syllable of the whole word (examples ná=mar=bal=... p. 49).
new_statements.exceptions: Clitics do not shift main stress ('a clitic will never carry main stress, but a suffix may', p. 56); monosyllabic roots lengthen to satisfy a two-mora word minimum (tii, soo); Spanish loan verbs (rellenar) keep Spanish stress (p. 199); serial-verb constructions form one phonological word with a single stress peak, while other verbal complexes have two peaks (p. 198); noun compounds have one stress peak vs. two in N+N phrases (p. 96).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem (root plus suffixes) within the phonological word; clitics attach outside it. Statements are for word-level citation forms; SVC/compound wordhood diagnosed by single stress peak. Older sources differ: Holmer 1947:23 describes accent as bearing 'evenly on all long... syllables' with no free accent (weight-driven, from accent marks in notes), and Prince 1913:482 calls stress irregular; the publisher blurb of Giannelli, Marotta & Pacini 2002 calls the system fundamentally trochaic, consistent with Smith's penult rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Smith 2014 explicitly describes the Guna 'spoken and understood to originate from the coastal communities of Guna Yala' (San Blas coast/islands), i.e. sanb1242 proper, by a heritage-speaker linguist; he notes eastern/central/western Guna Yala and Bayano/Darién (Border/Paya Kuna, ISO kvn, Glottolog bord1248) dialect differences but treats coastal Guna as one variety. Holmer 1947 and Prince 1913 also concern San Blas Cuna ('Tule'), Holmer partly from others' written notes. Note WALS 'Kuna' (kun) is keyed to bord1248 although its sources (Holmer 1947, Sherzer 1983) are San Blas.

new_statements.citation: Smith, Wikaliler Daniel. 2014. A Grammar of Guna: A Community-Centered Approach. PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Austin, sec. 2.5 Stress, pp. 48-49.
new_statements.reading: Main stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the root; suffixes that lengthen the word can move it (o.mé-gwa, us.dúp.pu), enclitics never take it (án=mar=ga is initial-stressed as a trisyllable), so surface placement depends on morphological composition rather than syllable count alone. Holmer 1947:23 gives an older, weight-based account (accent on every heavy syllable, none on light open syllables). Prince 1913:482 calls stress irregular and suffix-sensitive. Together these support the earlier audit's S2-SCOPE-EXIT (morphology-conditioned / weight-sensitive) rather than a single fixed-position code.

sources.citation: Holmer, Nils M. 1947. Critical and Comparative Grammar of the Cuna Language. Etnologiska Studier 14. Göteborg: Etnografiska Museet. xiv+219 pp. (archive.org EtnologiskaStudier14, CC0 upload by the museum)
sources.quote: Concerning the Cuna stress system, we may safely say that it depends altogether on the nature of the syllables. That this is so, and that no free accentuation (as in Siouan and Algonkin) exists, appears with sufficient clarity from the notes, where often two or three accents are marked in the same word (or on the vowels of consecutive syllables). The accent thus bears evenly on all long vowels or short vowels followed by a double or geminated consonant, or, in general, on long syllables. There is no accent on short vowels in open syllables [...] Furthermore, final closed syllables are never marked with an accent and consequently unstressed
sources.note: Sec. 4 'Syllabification and Accent' (pp. 19-24), p. 23: 'Concerning the Cuna stress system, we may safely say that it depends altogether on the nature of the syllables... no free accentuation... exists... The accent thus bears evenly on all long vowels or short vowels followed by a double or geminated consonant, or, in general, on long syllables. There is no accent on short vowels in open syllables'; final closed syllables never accented; a penult vowel loses stress before a vowel in the ultima; suffixes and enclitics are part of the 'stress unit'; compound members are separate stress units.…
